reasoning: The PKGBUILD is a standard prebuilt binary package that downloads pinned tarballs from the official upstream GitHub repository (github.com/earendil-works/pi) with proper sha256 checksums. No malicious behavior occurs during makepkg. The only 'unsafe' finding (qwen's flag on inline-bash.ts) is a classic false positive: it's an example extension in the upstream source tree that demonstrates the application's shell-execution feature. This code is never executed during package build or install—it's application payload shipped to /opt. Per the threat model, 'what the application does when it runs is the vendor's product, not an injection.'
disagreement_analysis: The disagreement stems from qwen reviewing example extension source files (inline-bash.ts) and misclassifying application functionality as a supply-chain injection. Deepseek's file selection failed (LLMResponseError), causing it to review different files (export-html utilities instead of extensions), but this didn't affect the verdict since those files were also safe. The openrouter/free report is advisory-only and had a parsing error on marked.min.js.
coverage_issues: deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash: File selection failed with LLMResponseError, fell back to highest-priority files, missing the extensions directory entirely
openrouter/free: Same file selection failure, plus parsing error on marked.min.js
false_positives: qwen flagged src/pi/examples/extensions/inline-bash.ts as 'Arbitrary command execution' - this is an example extension demonstrating the coding agent's shell feature, never executed during makepkg. It's upstream application code, not an AUR injection. The file lives in examples/ and is installed as part of the application payload, not run during build.
learnings: For -bin packages shipping prebuilt binaries, the audit tool should deprioritize or skip upstream application source files (especially under examples/, docs/, src/) that are merely installed as payload and never executed during makepkg

File selection needs better heuristics to distinguish 'code executed during packaging' from 'code shipped as application payload' - the current priority ranking surfaced example extensions over more relevant files
Models need stronger prompting that application features (like a coding agent's ability to run shell commands) are not supply-chain injections, even when they involve exec/spawn patterns
File selection failures (LLMResponseError) should trigger a retry or fallback that still covers high-risk directories like build scripts and install hooks, not just alphabetical priority
